notes:
Task and constraints: `findContestMatch(n)` receives a power-of-two team count and returns the full bracket string, pairing the current first and last teams in every round.
Idea: Store team labels as strings, then repeatedly replace the list with pair strings until one entry remains.
Technique and why it applies: The comprehension uses `teams[i]` and `teams[-1-i]` for the outer pairings; each round halves the list, matching the tournament structure directly.
Invariant: Before each round, `teams` contains the bracket expressions for the teams or matches still awaiting pairing, in their original bracket order.
Edge cases: For `n = 1`, the loop is skipped and the sole label is returned; for larger valid inputs, each round pairs exactly half as many entries.
Complexity: The supplied analysis states O(n) time and O(n log n) space; the constructed bracket text grows across logarithmically many rounds.
complexity_reason: The list length halves each round, and each generated parenthesized string preserves every team's label in bracket order.

notes:
Task and constraints: `findContestMatch(int n)` constructs a tournament bracket for a power-of-two number of teams, pairing outermost entries until one bracket remains.
Idea: Initialize `teams` with labels `1` through `n`, then build a fresh `next` list from symmetric entries in each round.
Technique and why it applies: `teams.get(i)` pairs with `teams.get(teams.size() - 1 - i)`; replacing `teams` with `next` ensures matches from one round become the entries for the next.
Invariant: At each loop boundary, `teams` holds the correctly ordered unresolved teams or match expressions for that round.
Edge cases: When `n` is one, no round executes and `teams.get(0)` returns `1`; the power-of-two constraint ensures every nonfinal round has an even number of entries.
Complexity: The supplied analysis gives O(n) time and O(n) space, excluding the details of the accumulated output string.
complexity_reason: Each loop iteration creates exactly half as many entries by pairing symmetric indices in the current list.

notes:
Task and constraints: `findCircleNum(isConnected)` counts connected components in an undirected graph represented by an n-by-n adjacency matrix.
Idea: Scan every vertex and start an iterative depth-first search whenever a vertex has not yet been visited.
Technique and why it applies: `seen` prevents repeated visits, while `stack` holds discovered vertices; examining `isConnected[u]` reveals all neighbors of the popped vertex `u`.
Invariant: Every vertex in `seen` belongs to a component already counted, and each unvisited `start` begins exactly one new component.
Edge cases: An empty matrix returns zero; isolated vertices each contribute a province; marking neighbors when pushed avoids duplicate stack entries.
Complexity: O(n²) time scans adjacency-matrix rows, and O(n) auxiliary space stores `seen` and the DFS stack.
complexity_reason: The outer loop starts one search per unseen vertex, while each search examines the corresponding matrix row.

notes:
Task and constraints: `findCircleNum(int[][] isConnected)` returns the number of connected components in an undirected graph stored as an adjacency matrix.
Idea: Iterate over each possible `start`; if unseen, increment `provinces` and traverse its component with an `ArrayDeque` stack.
Technique and why it applies: `isConnected[u][v] == 1` identifies an edge, and `seen[v]` is set before `stack.push(v)` so a vertex is queued only once.
Invariant: All vertices marked in `seen` are reachable from one of the counted starts, and no component is counted twice.
Edge cases: A zero-sized matrix returns zero; isolated vertices each create a component; the input is assumed to represent an undirected graph as stated.
Complexity: O(n²) time checks matrix entries, and O(n) auxiliary space holds the boolean array and traversal stack.
complexity_reason: Every component is initiated only at an unseen start, and each vertex is pushed at most once.

notes:
Task and constraints: `checkRecord(s)` accepts an attendance string only when it has fewer than two absences and no three consecutive late marks.
Idea: Combine a count of `A` characters with a substring check for `LLL`.
Technique and why it applies: `s.count('A') < 2` enforces the absence rule, and `'LLL' not in s` rejects every string containing a late streak of length three or more.
Invariant: The returned Boolean is true exactly when both independent attendance conditions hold.
Edge cases: Empty strings and strings without `A` or `LLL` pass; two or more `A` characters or any three-character `LLL` window fail.
Complexity: O(n) time scans the string for both checks, and O(1) auxiliary space is used apart from implementation-level temporary objects.
complexity_reason: Both predicates must be true, so either two absences or one triple-L substring immediately makes the record invalid.

notes:
Task and constraints: `checkRecord(String s)` rejects attendance records with at least two absences or three consecutive late marks.
Idea: Scan each character once, maintaining an `absences` counter and checking whether the current character completes an `LLL` streak.
Technique and why it applies: `s.charAt(i)` identifies the current mark; the counter returns false at the second `A`, while the `i >= 2` guard makes the two preceding-character checks safe.
Invariant: Before each iteration, `absences` counts the `A` characters seen so far, and no already-scanned position contains a rejected three-L streak unless the method has returned.
Edge cases: Strings shorter than three characters never enter the triple-L condition; empty input returns true; the method exits early when a rule is violated.
Complexity: O(n) time in the worst case and O(1) auxiliary space are required.
complexity_reason: The index guard protects both previous-character accesses, and the absence counter stops at the second A.

notes:
Task and constraints: `optimalDivision(nums)` inserts division operators and parentheses into a positive integer list while preserving order and maximizing the result.
Idea: Handle one and two elements directly; for three or more, place every element after the first inside one parenthesized denominator.
Technique and why it applies: The expression `nums[0] + "/(" + "/".join(map(str, nums[1:])) + ")"` yields `a/(b/c/d)`, making the denominator a nested quotient and maximizing the value for positive inputs.
Invariant: The generated expression includes every input value once and in its original order, with the first value as the numerator.
Edge cases: A single value needs no operator; two values need only one slash; positive inputs avoid division-by-zero concerns.
Complexity: O(n) time builds and joins the output, and O(n) space stores the sliced values and resulting expression.
complexity_reason: For positive numbers, grouping all divisors after the first creates the largest quotient without reordering any element.

notes:
Task and constraints: `optimalDivision(int[] nums)` returns a maximum-value division expression while preserving the positive integers' order.
Idea: Return direct forms for arrays of length one or two, and otherwise append the first number followed by a parenthesized division of all remaining numbers.
Technique and why it applies: `StringBuilder out` assembles `nums[0] + "/("` and appends each later `nums[i]`, inserting slashes between denominator terms before closing `)`.
Invariant: Every array element appears exactly once in sequence, and for length at least three the first element is divided by the grouped remaining expression.
Edge cases: Length one returns only the number; length two returns `a/b`; the positive-number assumption prevents zero denominators.
Complexity: O(n) time appends all values and delimiters, and O(n) space is used for the constructed expression.
complexity_reason: Grouping the remaining positive values in parentheses makes their quotient the denominator and maximizes the overall result.

notes:
Task and constraints: `reverseWords(s)` reverses characters inside each word while retaining the original word sequence and spaces.
Idea: Split on the literal space, reverse each resulting substring with slicing, then join the pieces using one literal space.
Technique and why it applies: `word[::-1]` reverses a word, and `s.split(' ')` preserves empty fields created by repeated or leading spaces, so joining retains spacing positions.
Invariant: Each word segment is reversed independently, while the order and number of space separators remain unchanged.
Edge cases: Empty input produces an empty result; repeated spaces create empty segments that remain in place; punctuation is reversed along with its word's characters.
Complexity: O(n) time processes each character a constant number of times, and O(n) space holds the split words and output.
complexity_reason: Splitting on a literal space rather than generic whitespace preserves consecutive spaces as empty word segments.

notes:
Task and constraints: `reverseWords(String s)` reverses every word's characters without changing word order or the spaces between words.
Idea: Split using a single-space delimiter with trailing empty strings retained, reverse each array element, then join with spaces.
Technique and why it applies: `s.split(" ", -1)` preserves trailing empty segments, `new StringBuilder(words[i]).reverse()` reverses each segment, and `String.join(" ", words)` reconstructs the sentence.
Invariant: The `words` array retains one segment for each space-separated position, and only the characters inside individual segments are reversed.
Edge cases: Empty strings and repeated, leading, or trailing spaces require retaining empty segments; punctuation stays within and reverses with its segment.
Complexity: O(n) time visits the characters during splitting, reversal, and joining, and O(n) space stores the segments and result.
complexity_reason: The negative split limit retains trailing empty fields, which is necessary to preserve trailing spaces in the sentence.

notes:
Task and constraints: `maxDepth(root)` returns the number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path in an N-ary tree, with an empty tree having depth zero.
Idea: Return zero for `None`; otherwise compute one plus the maximum depth among `root.children`.
Technique and why it applies: The recursive generator calls `self.maxDepth(child)` for every child, while `max(..., default=0)` correctly handles a leaf with no children.
Invariant: Each recursive call returns the maximum depth of its subtree, so adding one accounts for the current node.
Edge cases: `root is None` returns zero; a leaf returns one; the recursion follows each child subtree once.
Complexity: O(n) time visits each node once, and O(h) auxiliary stack space is used for tree height h.
complexity_reason: A leaf's child-depth maximum defaults to zero, making its returned depth exactly one.

notes:
Task and constraints: `maxDepth(Node root)` finds the longest root-to-leaf node count in an N-ary tree and returns zero for a null root.
Idea: Recursively compute each child's depth, track the largest in `best`, and return `best + 1` for the current node.
Technique and why it applies: `for (Node child : root.children)` explores every child; `Math.max` keeps the deepest result without storing all child depths.
Invariant: `best` is the maximum depth among children already processed, and the method's return value includes the current node.
Edge cases: A null root returns zero; a leaf leaves `best` at zero and returns one; recursion depth follows the tallest branch.
Complexity: O(n) time visits each node once, and O(h) auxiliary space is used by recursive calls for height h.
complexity_reason: The accumulator `best` records the deepest child so far, and adding one counts the current node.

notes:
Task and constraints: `subarraySum(nums, k)` counts contiguous subarrays whose elements sum exactly to `k`, including arrays with negative values.
Idea: Maintain a running prefix `total` and a frequency map `freq` of earlier prefix sums; add the frequency of `total - k` to `answer` at each position.
Technique and why it applies: The initial `freq = {0: 1}` accounts for subarrays beginning at index zero, and `freq[total]` is incremented only after matching earlier prefixes are counted.
Invariant: Before processing the current prefix, `freq[p]` records how many prior prefix positions have sum `p`, so each matching earlier prefix identifies one valid subarray ending here.
Edge cases: Negative values are supported because no sliding-window monotonicity is assumed; repeated prefix sums correctly contribute multiple subarrays; an empty list returns zero.
Complexity: O(n) expected time uses hash-map operations per element, and O(n) space stores distinct prefix sums.
complexity_reason: Looking up `total - k` before recording `total` prevents the current prefix from being paired with itself when k is zero.

notes:
Task and constraints: `subarraySum(int[] nums, int k)` counts contiguous subarrays with sum `k` and must work when values can be negative.
Idea: Use a `Map<Integer, Integer> freq` to count previous prefix sums and maintain `total` and `answer` while scanning `nums`.
Technique and why it applies: `freq.put(0, 1)` seeds the empty prefix; each iteration adds `freq.getOrDefault(total - k, 0)` to `answer`, then increments the frequency for `total`.
Invariant: `freq` contains counts only for prefix positions before the current endpoint, making every lookup correspond to a distinct candidate subarray.
Edge cases: Negative numbers do not break the prefix-sum method; duplicate prefix totals must retain their full frequency; empty input returns zero.
Complexity: O(n) expected time assumes constant-average `HashMap` operations, and O(n) space stores prefix-sum frequencies.
complexity_reason: The map must count duplicate prefix totals because each earlier occurrence can define a different valid subarray.

notes:
Task and constraints: `arrayPairSum(nums)` partitions an even-sized list into pairs to maximize the sum of each pair's smaller member.
Idea: Sort `nums` and sum the values at even indices, `nums[::2]`.
Technique and why it applies: In sorted order, pairing adjacent values makes each even-indexed value the smaller member of its pair; this arrangement minimizes losses to the pair minimums.
Invariant: After sorting, indices `(0,1)`, `(2,3)`, and so on are paired, so the first value of each pair contributes to the answer.
Edge cases: Negative values are handled by sorting as well; the input length is assumed even; sorting mutates `nums` in place.
Complexity: O(n log n) time is dominated by sorting, and O(1) auxiliary space excluding the sorting implementation is the stated bound.
complexity_reason: Sorting places the strongest possible pair minima at even indices when each adjacent pair contributes its smaller value.

notes:
Task and constraints: `arrayPairSum(int[] nums)` maximizes the sum of pair minima when pairing all elements of an even-length array.
Idea: Sort `nums`, then add elements at indices `0, 2, 4, ...` to `answer`.
Technique and why it applies: `Arrays.sort(nums)` orders values so adjacent pairs have the smallest member at each even index; the loop advances by two to take exactly those members.
Invariant: At the start of each loop iteration, `answer` is the sum of minima for all adjacent sorted pairs before index `i`.
Edge cases: Negative integers are valid; the array is modified by sorting; the input length must be even for complete pairing.
Complexity: O(n log n) time is dominated by `Arrays.sort`, and O(1) auxiliary space excluding the sorting implementation is the stated bound.
complexity_reason: Adjacent pairing after sorting maximizes the sum of minima by preventing larger values from being wasted as pair minima.

notes:
Task and constraints: `findTilt(root)` sums the absolute difference between left and right subtree sums for every node in a binary tree.
Idea: Use the nested `total(node)` helper to compute subtree sums in postorder while accumulating each node's tilt in `tilt`.
Technique and why it applies: `total` returns zero for `None`, recursively obtains `left` and `right`, adds `abs(left - right)` to `tilt`, then returns `node.val + left + right`.
Invariant: Once `total(node)` returns, it has computed the exact sum of that subtree and has added the tilt contribution of every node within it.
Edge cases: An empty tree returns zero; leaves have tilt zero; each subtree is traversed once, avoiding repeated sum calculations.
Complexity: O(n) time visits each node once, and O(h) auxiliary space is used by recursion for height h.
complexity_reason: Postorder ensures both child sums are available before `abs(left - right)` contributes to the total tilt.

notes:
Task and constraints: `findTilt(TreeNode root)` returns the sum of absolute left-versus-right subtree-sum differences across all nodes.
Idea: Reset the instance field `tilt`, call `sum(root)`, and return the accumulated total.
Technique and why it applies: `sum(TreeNode node)` recursively computes `left` and `right`, adds `Math.abs(left - right)` to `tilt`, and returns `node.val + left + right` to its parent.
Invariant: Each `sum` call returns the subtree's complete value sum after recording the tilt for every node in that subtree.
Edge cases: A null root yields zero; leaves contribute zero tilt; resetting `tilt` in `findTilt` prevents values from a previous invocation leaking into a later call.
Complexity: O(n) time processes every node once, and O(h) auxiliary space is consumed by recursion for tree height h.
complexity_reason: Resetting `tilt` before traversal is essential because the accumulator is stored on the reusable Solution instance.

notes:
Task and constraints: `matrixReshape(mat, r, c)` changes the dimensions while preserving row-major element order, returning the original matrix when element counts differ.
Idea: Compare `m * n` with `r * c`, flatten `mat` into `flat`, and slice the flattened sequence into `r` rows of `c` elements.
Technique and why it applies: The comprehension `[x for row in mat for x in row]` follows row-major order, and `flat[i * c:(i + 1) * c]` builds each target row without reordering values.
Invariant: If reshape proceeds, `flat` contains exactly the original matrix elements in row-major order and each output row consumes the next `c` values.
Edge cases: A mismatched element count returns `mat` unchanged; the implementation assumes a nonempty rectangular matrix because it reads `mat[0]`; valid dimensions must match the element count.
Complexity: O(mn) time copies and partitions all elements, and O(mn) space stores the flattened list and reshaped output.
complexity_reason: The product check ensures slicing can distribute every original element into exactly r rows of c values.

notes:
Task and constraints: `matrixReshape(int[][] mat, int r, int c)` reshapes a matrix while preserving row-major order, or returns `mat` when the element count changes.
Idea: Compute `m` and `n`, verify `m * n == r * c`, then map each flattened index into target and source coordinates.
Technique and why it applies: `out[i / c][i % c]` selects the target cell, while `mat[i / n][i % n]` selects the corresponding original cell in row-major order.
Invariant: After processing flattened index `i`, all earlier indices have been copied to matching positions in `out` without changing their order.
Edge cases: A product mismatch returns the original array reference; the code assumes a nonempty rectangular matrix and positive target dimensions when reshaping; matching element counts are required.
Complexity: O(mn) time copies every element once, and O(mn) space allocates the output matrix.
complexity_reason: Integer division and remainder convert each flat position into its correct row and column in both dimensions.
